docs.text:
Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute. — Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
Every Scala codebase carries a second program, written in prose. It sits in the doc comments above classes and methods, and it explains what the code means: what a field holds, what a parameter is for, why an exception gets thrown. The compiler reads it once, mostly to throw it away, and scaladoc turns it into a web site. Then it rests.
That’s a waste, because the prose is often exactly what other tools are missing. A JSON Schema derived from a case class can say that a field is a string, but not that it’s the name shown to other users. An OpenAPI spec knows the shape of a request, not its purpose. The purpose is right there in the source, one line above the shape.
This library puts that prose to work. It has four parts:
a model of what a doc comment says: its tags (@param, @return, …) and its markup (paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, code, links, bold and the rest) a parser that turns comment text into the model. It reads scaladoc’s wiki markup, HTML and javadoc’s inline tags, on the JVM and on Scala.js Scaladoc.of[T], which hands you the scaladoc of a type at compile time, in macros and type class derivation a compiler plugin (Scala 2) that embeds the scaladoc of classes into their bytecode, so it survives the trip into a jar
Here is the whole idea in a few lines. A case class documents itself, and the code asks it what it said:
import scaladoc._

object model {

  /** A user of the app.
    *
    * Users sign up with an e-mail address and can change their name later.
    *
    * @param name the name shown to other users
    * @param age  how old they are, in years
    */
  case class User(name: String, age: Int)
}

import model._

val doc = Scaladoc.of[User].get
doc.textSummary
// res0: Option[String] = Some(value = "A user of the app.")
doc.textParams
// res1: Map[String, String] = Map(
//   "name" -> "the name shown to other users",
//   "age" -> "how old they are, in years"
// )
textSummary is the first sentence, the one scaladoc itself would show in a list of members. textParams is what each field means. A schema generator needs nothing more to give every property a title and a description.

docs.text:
Talk is cheap. Show me the code. — Linus Torvalds
There are two ways in: the sbt plugin, which knows what each kind of module needs, or adding the dependencies by hand. The plugin is the shorter road, so it comes first.
docs.title: Getting started

docs.text:
Add sbt-scaladoc to project/plugins.sbt:
addSbtPlugin("io.github.andyglow" % "sbt-scaladoc" % "0.4.0")
and enable it on the modules that need it:
lazy val model = project
  .enablePlugins(ScaladocPlugin)
That’s it. What happens next depends on which Scala the module speaks, because Scala 2 and Scala 3 keep doc comments in very different places:
Scala 2 forgets doc comments once it’s done compiling, so the plugin adds the compiler plugin, which writes them into the bytecode before they’re lost. It also adds scaladoc-ast and scaladoc-parser. A module that only reads scaladoc, and has none of its own worth keeping, can set scaladocEmbed := false. Scala 3 keeps doc comments in its TASTy files, so no compiler plugin is needed (and none exists). The plugin adds scaladoc-ast, scaladoc-parser and -Yread-docs, the option that tells the compiler to load those comments for Scaladoc.of. Scala.js gets the _sjs1 libraries. The compiler plugin runs inside scalac, which is a JVM program however its output is used, so the JVM artifact serves Scala.js modules too.
The libraries get the plugin’s own version, and scaladocVersion overrides it. The other settings tune what the compiler plugin embeds:
Setting Default What it does scaladocVersion plugin’s the version of the libraries and the compiler plugin scaladocEmbed true Scala 2: embed scaladoc into bytecode with the compiler plugin scaladocIncludePaths none Scala 2: embed only classes from source files matching these globs scaladocExcludePaths none Scala 2: don’t embed classes from source files matching these globs scaladocIncludeClasses none Scala 2: embed only classes whose name matches these patterns scaladocExcludeClasses none Scala 2: don’t embed classes whose name matches these patterns
The patterns are explained in Choosing what to embed.
docs.title: With the sbt plugin

docs.text:
The libraries are two ordinary dependencies:
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-ast"    % "0.4.0"
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-parser" % "0.4.0"
To embed scaladoc into bytecode (Scala 2 only), add the compiler plugin as well. The parser is then only needed while compiling, so it can stay out of the runtime classpath:
addCompilerPlugin("io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-compiler-plugin" % "0.4.0")

libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-ast"    % "0.4.0"
libraryDependencies += "io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-parser" % "0.4.0" % Provided
On Scala 3, compile the modules that call Scaladoc.of with -Yread-docs:
scalacOptions += "-Yread-docs"
On Scala.js, use %%% for scaladoc-ast and scaladoc-parser. The compiler plugin stays %%.
Note The groupId changed in 0.1.0, from com.github.andyglow to io.github.andyglow. Versions up to 0.0.14 stay available under the old one. To upgrade from them, change the groupId along with the version.

A first look

docs.text:
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. — Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
A doc comment looks like prose, but it’s a small language with a grammar of its own. Scaladoc defined most of it: the * border, the @ tags, a wiki markup with ''italic'' and [[links]]. Over the years, comments picked up some HTML and a few habits from javadoc along the way, and real codebases contain all of it, often in the same comment.
The parser reads all of it, and this page walks through what it understands, from the outside in: first the comment as a whole, then its tags, then the markup inside them. Every example on this page is compiled and run when the site is built, so what you see after each snippet is what the parser really returns.
docs.title: Comment syntax
The comment

docs.text:
Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. — Andy Hunt and Dave Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer
A tag starts a line with @ and its name. Everything up to the next tag is its text, and the text before the first tag is the description. An @ in the middle of a line, as in an e-mail address or @tailrec, is just a character:
Scaladoc.fromString(
  """/** Sends mail to support@example.com, see `@tailrec`.
    |  *
    |  * @param to   who gets it
    |  * @param body what it says,
    |  *             over two lines
    |  * @throws java.io.IOException if the server is down
    |  * @return the message id
    |  */""".stripMargin).map(_.tags.map(_.productPrefix))
// res3: Either[ScaladocException, List[String]] = Right(
//   value = List("Description", "Param", "Param", "Throws", "Returns")
// )
These are the tags the model knows by name. Any other one, like @contentDiagram, comes back as an OtherTag with its name and text.
Tag Model Text the text before the first tag Description markup @constructor Constructor markup @param name Param(name, ...) markup @tparam name TypeParam(name, ...) markup @return (or @returns) Returns markup @throws type Throws(type, ...) markup @see, @note, @example See, Note, Example markup @usecase UseCase markup @todo, @deprecated, @migration Todo, Deprecated, Migration markup @author, @version, @since Author, Version, Since plain text @group id Group(id) none @groupname id GroupName(id, ...) plain text @groupdesc id GroupDescription(id, ...) markup @groupprio id n GroupPriority(id, n) a number @documentable, @inheritdoc Documentable, InheritDoc none anything else OtherTag(name, ...) markup
A tag without text is dropped, since it says nothing, with two exceptions that scaladoc makes as well: @deprecated deprecates even without a reason, and @throws IOException names an exception even without saying when.

docs.text:
Scaladoc renders comments to HTML, and this parser turns them into a model for other tools to use. A few choices follow from that difference, and a few from fixing what scaladoc leaves to warnings:
Monospace is literal. Scaladoc parses markup inside backticks; here the text of code stays as written. Unclosed markers are text. Scaladoc runs an unclosed '' to the end of the paragraph. Bold inside italic works. In ''a '''b''' c'', scaladoc ends the italic at the '''; here the bold nests. Broken tables aren’t tables. Without a valid delimiter row, scaladoc repairs the table and warns; here the lines stay text, which is what GitHub does and what scaladoc’s own source says it should do. HTML becomes the model. Scaladoc passes <b> on as HTML; here it’s Bold, and HTML in code blocks is left alone. {@literal} is text, as in javadoc. Scaladoc shows it as code. @define sees only its own comment, as described above.
docs.title: How this differs from scaladoc

docs.text:
The map is not the territory. — Alfred Korzybski
A parsed comment is a map of the comment, and like every map it leaves things out on purpose. The border is gone, and so are the exact spaces and how a list item was indented. What remains is what the comment says: which tags it has, and how its text is structured. This page is the legend of that map.
docs.title: The model

docs.text:
A Scaladoc is a list of tags, in the order they appear. The description, the text before the first tag, is a tag too. Most tags hold their text as Markup. A few, like @author or @since, hold plain strings, and some, like @documentable, hold nothing. The syntax page has the full list.
Tag      = Description       (Markup)
         | Constructor       (Markup)
         | Param             (String Markup)
         | TypeParam         (String Markup)
         | Returns           (Markup)
         | Throws            (String Markup)
         | See | Note | Example | UseCase | Todo | Deprecated | Migration   (Markup)
         | Author | Version | Since                                       (String)
         | Group             (String)
         | GroupName         (String String)
         | GroupDescription  (String Markup)
         | GroupPriority     (String Int)
         | Documentable
         | InheritDoc
         | OtherTag          (String Markup)

Scaladoc = List Tag
docs.title: Scaladoc and its tags

docs.text:
Markup comes in two kinds: blocks, which stack on top of each other, and spans, which run inline within a block. A Document holds blocks, and a tag’s text is always a Document:
Span     = PlainText   (String)
         | Monospace   (String)
         | Italic      (List Span)
         | Bold        (List Span)
         | Underline   (List Span)
         | Superscript (List Span)
         | Subscript   (List Span)
         | Link        (String (List Span))        -- target, title
         | HtmlTag     (String)                    -- an HTML tag the model has no node for

Markup   = Span
         | Paragraph     (List Span)
         | Heading       (Level (List Span))       -- Level: One to Six
         | CodeBlock     (String)
         | UnorderedList (List Document)           -- each item: its text and nested lists
         | OrderedList   (List Document Style)     -- Style: Decimal, LowerRoman, UpperRoman, LowerAlpha, UpperAlpha
         | Table         (Row (List Alignment) (List Row))   -- a Row: one Paragraph a cell
         | HorizontalRule
         | Document      (List Markup)
The spans that hold other spans can nest without limit, so walking the model is naturally recursive. Here is a function that collects every link target in a piece of markup, however deep it sits:
def links(m: Markup): List[String] = m match {
  case Link(target, title)     => target :: title.flatMap(links)
  case Document(elements)      => elements.flatMap(links)
  case Paragraph(spans)        => spans.flatMap(links)
  case Heading(_, spans)       => spans.flatMap(links)
  case x: HasSpans             => x.spans.flatMap(links)
  case x: ListBlock            => x.items.flatMap(links)
  case Table(header, _, rows)  => (header :: rows).flatMap(_.cells).flatMap(links)
  case _                       => Nil
}

Scaladoc.fromString(
  """/** See [[scala.Option]].
    |  *
    |  *   - '''also [[scala.Either]]'''
    |  */""".stripMargin).map(_.descriptions.flatMap(links))
// res0: Either[ScaladocException, Seq[String]] = Right(
//   value = List("scala.Option", "scala.Either")
// )
Building markup by hand is just as direct. Every span has a shorthand for the common case of a single piece of text:
Paragraph(PlainText("Use "), Bold("this"), PlainText(" or "), Link("scala.Option"))
// res1: Paragraph = Paragraph(
//   markup = List(
//     PlainText(value = "Use "),
//     Bold(spans = List(PlainText(value = "this"))),
//     PlainText(value = " or "),
//     Link(target = "scala.Option", title = List())
//   )
// )
docs.title: Markup
Text, when markup is too much
Scaladoc.of

docs.text:
The Scala 2 compiler keeps a comment only while it compiles the source file the comment is in, and forgets it afterwards. Scaladoc.of therefore checks three places, in this order:
macro attachments, where other macros may have left a comment the @ScaladocCarrier annotation that the compiler plugin adds to the bytecode of a documented class. This is what makes classes from other modules and from jars work the source code, when the class is compiled in the same run as the call
The third place is fragile. An incremental compile that doesn’t recompile the class’s file loses the comment. For anything beyond a single module, the compiler plugin is the reliable way.
docs.title: On Scala 2

docs.text:
Scala 3 keeps doc comments in TASTy, the format it stores type information in, and Scaladoc.of reads them from Symbol.docstring. By default, though, the compiler only loads the comments of the sources it compiles in the current run. To read them from TASTy as well (other modules, jars, and files skipped by an incremental compile), compile the module that calls Scaladoc.of with -Yread-docs:
scalacOptions += "-Yread-docs"
The sbt plugin adds it on Scala 3 modules.
docs.title: On Scala 3

docs.text: A comment whose * border wanders from line to line is usually a sign of a botched edit. Scaladoc.of checks the alignment, on Scala 2 and on Scala 3 alike, and reports a comment it can’t make sense of as a compile error at the call site, with the comment and the reason. A comment without borders is fine; only a border that’s there gets checked.
docs.title: A misaligned comment is a compile error
From a string

docs.text:
The palest ink is better than the best memory. — Chinese proverb
The Scala 2 compiler has a short memory. It reads every doc comment while it compiles a file, then lets go of it, and nothing of the comment reaches the bytecode. A tool that looks at your classes later, from another module or out of a jar, finds the types intact and the prose gone.
The compiler plugin writes the prose down before it’s forgotten. For every documented class, it:
validates the comment. One the parser can’t read, like one with a misaligned border, is reported as a warning in the scaladoc category and isn’t embedded. -Xfatal-warnings, or -Wconf:cat=scaladoc:e on 2.13, turns it into an error packs the comment into a @ScaladocCarrier annotation on the class, which stays in the bytecode
Scaladoc.of finds the annotation, so it works for classes from any module or jar compiled with the plugin. The plugin is for Scala 2.12 and 2.13. Scala 3 doesn’t need it, since it keeps comments in TASTy on its own.
The sbt plugin adds it on Scala 2 modules. By hand:
addCompilerPlugin("io.github.andyglow" %% "scaladoc-compiler-plugin" % "0.4.0")
docs.title: Compiler plugin

docs.text:
By default the plugin embeds the scaladoc of every documented class. That’s often more than needed, and a comment meant for the team may not be meant for every jar. Include and exclude patterns narrow it down. With sbt-scaladoc they’re settings:
scaladocIncludePaths   := Seq("**/model/**")
scaladocIncludeClasses := Seq("com.acme.api.*")
scaladocExcludePaths   := Seq("**/generated/**")
scaladocExcludeClasses := Seq("com.acme.**.internal.*")
Without it, they’re options of the compiler plugin, and each can be given several times:
scalacOptions ++= Seq(
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:include:path:**/model/**",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:include:class:com.acme.api.*",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:exclude:path:**/generated/**",
  "-P:scaladoc-compiler-plugin:exclude:class:com.acme.**.internal.*"
)
Option Matches include:path:<glob> source files whose path matches the glob exclude:path:<glob> the same, to leave out include:class:<pattern> classes whose fully qualified name matches the pattern exclude:class:<pattern> the same, to leave out
The rules, in the order they’re applied:
Without any include, every class is included. With some, a class is included if its file matches an include:path or its name matches an include:class. An exclude always wins over an include. Path globs use java.nio glob syntax and are matched against the absolute path of the source file, so they usually start with **/. In class patterns, * matches within one segment of the name, ** across segments, and **. zero or more packages: com.acme.**.internal.* matches both com.acme.internal.Secret and com.acme.a.b.internal.Secret. Nested classes are written with dots, as in com.acme.Outer.Inner. A malformed option fails the compilation, rather than quietly embedding everything.
docs.title: Choosing what to embed

docs.text:
No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it’s not the same river and he’s not the same man. — attributed to Heraclitus
0.4 is the release where the parser learned the rest of scaladoc’s syntax: nested markup, link titles, lists, tables, rules, HTML, javadoc’s inline tags and @define. A model that couldn’t hold those had to grow, and code that takes it apart needs a few changes. Code that only builds markup, or only reads text through the text* helpers, mostly doesn’t.
docs.title: Migrating to 0.4

docs.text:
Italic, Bold, Underline, Superscript and Subscript held a String. They now hold a List[Span], so markup can nest. Building one from a string still works, through a shorthand on each companion:
Bold("text")                           // still compiles, now Bold(List(PlainText("text")))
Pattern matches on the string need updating:
// 0.3
case Bold(text)        => text
// 0.4
case b @ Bold(spans)   => b.trimmed.plainString     // or walk the spans
Monospace still holds a String: code is taken literally.
docs.title: Spans hold spans

docs.text: Heading(level, text: String) is now Heading(level, spans: List[Span]), so a title can have markup. Heading(One, "Title") and Heading(1, "Title") still build one. A heading’s title is also trimmed now: = Title = gives "Title", not " Title ".
docs.title: Headings hold spans

docs.text: Link(value: String) held whatever was between the brackets, so [[https://x.y Site]] gave Link("https://x.y Site"). It’s now Link(target: String, title: List[Span]), and that link gives Link("https://x.y", List(PlainText("Site"))). Link("scala.Option") still builds one without a title.
docs.title: Links have a target and a title

docs.text:
Code that matches on Markup exhaustively will hear from the compiler about these:
UnorderedList and OrderedList, whose items are Documents Table, with its rows and column alignments HorizontalRule HtmlTag, a span for HTML tags the model has no node for
docs.title: New nodes

docs.text:
The parser now understands more, so some comments that came back as plain text before don’t anymore:
a line like - item is a list item, and | a | b | lines with a delimiter row are a table <b>, <code>, < and the like are markup and characters, not text {@link X} is a link, {@code x} monospace $name is replaced when the comment defines name with @define
docs.title: Text that changed

docs.text:
0.4 also fixes a number of things that 0.3 got wrong. They don’t change the API, but they do change what some comments parse to:
@return is the returns tag, as in scaladoc. @returns still works a tag starts a line, so foo@bar.com is text; and nothing inside {{{ }}} is a tag @throws java.io.IOException keeps its full exception type @deprecated and @throws X are kept without text the * border is optional an unclosed marker, like the ^ of x^2, is text instead of an error that loses the comment one space after the border belongs to the border, and text is always in a Paragraph code blocks lose the indentation all their lines share Tag.Description’s field is markup; the misspelled makrup stays as a deprecated alias
docs.title: Fixes that change results
